name: Kimura from Knee on Belly
description: Master the Kimura from Knee on Belly in BJJ. Learn how KOB pressure creates shoulder lock opportunities through forced defensive reactions and grip exposure.
summary: The Kimura from Knee on Belly is a figure-four shoulder lock applied from top, where crushing knee pressure forces the bottom player to expose an arm that is then trapped and rotated against the shoulder joint.
target_area: Shoulder joint, rotator cuff, and shoulder capsule
overview:
The Kimura from Knee on Belly exploits the natural defensive reactions that KOB pressure creates. When the bottom player pushes against the knee or reaches across their body to alleviate diaphragm pressure, their far arm becomes exposed for figure-four grip capture. The elevated hip position of Knee on Belly provides superior rotational leverage compared to side control or guard-based kimuras, allowing greater torque on the shoulder joint with less effort. The bottom player faces a compounding dilemma: absorb the crushing knee pressure and risk respiratory distress, or push the knee away and expose their arms to the shoulder lock.

The finishing mechanics differ from other positions because the top player can choose to finish in place by driving the captured wrist toward the mat while maintaining knee pressure, or step off to north-south for a more controlled rotational finish. The north-south transition removes the bottom player's bridging ability and creates a tighter arc of rotation on the shoulder. The grip capture itself benefits from gravity — the top player's weight assists in pinning the opponent's elbow while the figure-four controls the wrist. Competition data consistently shows this as one of the highest-percentage kimura entries in the sport, particularly effective after the top player has broken down the bottom player's defensive frames with sustained KOB pressure.

injury_risks.injury: Rotator cuff tear (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis)

injury_risks.recovery_time: 6-12 weeks for strain, 3-6 months for rupture

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum in training, allowing partner time to recognize danger and tap
tap_signals: Verbal tap (saying 'tap' or making any verbal distress sound)
Physical hand tap (multiple taps with free hand)
Physical foot tap (multiple taps with either foot)
Any distress signal including screaming or unusual sounds
release_protocol: Immediately stop all rotational pressure the instant tap is felt or heard
Return the arm toward neutral position (externally rotate back to starting position)
Allow partner to self-assess shoulder mobility before continuing
Never release suddenly or allow arm to spring back forcefully
training_restrictions: Never spike or jerk the submission - rotation must be smooth and controlled
Never use competition speed or surprise attacks in training
Always ensure partner has at least one hand free to tap
Do not apply while partner is in awkward body position that prevents tapping
Never combine with weight pressure that restricts breathing while finishing
Respect immediate taps without testing partner's pain tolerance

variations_and_setups.description: Maintain heavy KOB pressure until the bottom player pushes on your knee with their far hand. The moment they extend their arm, capture the wrist and secure the figure-four grip while maintaining knee contact.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the bottom player is reactive and consistently pushes against the knee to relieve pressure

variations_and_setups.description: After securing the figure-four grip from KOB, step your knee off the torso and rotate toward north-south position. This removes the bottom player's bridging power and creates a tighter rotational arc on the shoulder for a higher-percentage finish.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the bottom player has strong bridging ability or when the in-place finish is being defended by straightening the arm

variations_and_setups.description: Instead of attacking the far arm, target the near-side arm when the bottom player reaches across their body to establish an underhook or frame. Drop your weight to pin their elbow and secure the figure-four on the near wrist.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the bottom player's near arm is exposed from reaching for underhooks or defensive frames

attacker.name: Kimura from Knee on Belly Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack the Kimura from Knee on Belly. Step-by-step guide covering grip capture, pressure maintenance, and finishing mechanics from the dominant top position.
attacker.overview: Attacking the Kimura from Knee on Belly requires understanding how to weaponize positional pressure as a submission setup. The top player uses the crushing diaphragm pressure of KOB to force defensive arm reactions, then captures the exposed limb in a figure-four grip. The elevated hip position provides a mechanical advantage over ground-level kimura entries because gravity assists both the grip capture and the rotational finish. The attacker must balance maintaining enough KOB pressure to provoke reactions while staying light enough to transition into the grip capture without losing position. The finish can be executed in place or by stepping off to north-south, and recognizing which option to use based on the defender's body positioning is what separates high-percentage finishes from failed attempts.
key_principles: Use KOB pressure as the primary submission setup — the diaphragm pressure forces arm exposure
Capture the figure-four grip before committing to the finish — premature rotation without control loses the position
Pin the opponent's elbow to their body or the mat before applying rotational force on the wrist
Maintain chest-forward weight distribution during the grip fight to prevent guard recovery
Recognize when to finish in place versus stepping off to north-south based on opponent's defensive posture
Control the wrist at the point of capture — losing wrist control means losing the submission
setup_requirements: Established Knee on Belly with knee on solar plexus and base leg posted wide for stability
Near-side collar grip or cross-face control preventing opponent from turning into you
Far-side pants or belt grip controlling opponent's hip rotation and preventing guard recovery
Opponent's far arm exposed or accessible — either extended from pushing or positioned across their body
Sufficient base to transition from pressure position to grip capture without losing top control

execution_steps.description: Drive your knee into the opponent's solar plexus with your weight directed forward through the contact point. Maintain collar and pants grips while keeping your base leg wide. The goal is to create enough respiratory distress to force a defensive arm reaction.
execution_steps.timing: Hold pressure for 3-5 seconds until opponent reacts

execution_steps.action: Identify and capture the target arm
execution_steps.description: Watch for the opponent's far arm extending to push your knee or reaching across their body. The moment the arm is exposed, release your pants grip and capture their wrist with your far hand, controlling it palm-down against their body or the mat.
execution_steps.timing: Immediate — within 1 second of arm exposure

execution_steps.description: Thread your near hand under the opponent's captured arm and grip your own wrist to complete the figure-four lock. Your forearm should be positioned against the back of their wrist with their elbow bent at approximately ninety degrees. Squeeze your elbows tight to your body.
execution_steps.timing: 1-2 seconds — fast grip completion prevents arm extraction

execution_steps.action: Pin the elbow and consolidate control
execution_steps.description: Drive the opponent's elbow toward their hip using downward pressure from your figure-four. Their upper arm must be pinned against their torso or the mat. Without elbow control, they can straighten their arm and escape the grip. Use your chest weight to assist the pin.

Evaluate whether to finish in place or step off to north-south. If the opponent is flat and immobilized, finish in place by rotating the wrist toward the mat. If they are bridging or creating space, step your knee off and rotate toward north-south to eliminate their bridging leverage.
execution_steps.timing: Decision within 1-2 seconds of elbow pin

execution_steps.description: With the elbow pinned and figure-four secure, slowly rotate the opponent's wrist away from their body in an arc toward their feet. Keep the rotation in the plane of the shoulder joint. Apply pressure progressively, giving the opponent time to tap. The finish comes from rotating the forearm past the plane of the back.
execution_steps.timing: 3-5 seconds of progressive pressure — never jerk or spike

common_counters.counter: Opponent grabs their own belt or pants to anchor the arm against rotation
common_counters.your_response: Peel their grip by driving your knee across their forearm or transition to an Americana by reversing the rotational direction. Alternatively, step to north-south where the angle change weakens their grip anchor.

common_counters.counter: Opponent straightens their arm to prevent the figure-four lock from closing
common_counters.your_response: Transition to an armbar by swinging your leg over their straightened arm, or re-bend the arm by driving their wrist toward their ear using your body weight. A straight arm is an armbar opportunity.

common_counters.counter: Opponent bridges and rolls toward you to relieve pressure and pull you into guard
common_counters.your_response: Post your base leg wide and sprawl your hips to prevent the roll. If they succeed in turning, maintain the figure-four grip and transition to a kimura from top position in their guard.

common_counters.counter: Opponent shrimps away and recovers knee shield or half guard
common_counters.your_response: Follow their hip movement and re-establish heavy top pressure. If the kimura grip is still intact, finish from the new position. If the grip is lost, return to side control or KOB and reset the attack.

common_errors.error: Releasing KOB pressure too early before securing the figure-four grip
common_errors.consequence: Opponent regains composure and frames effectively, preventing arm capture and allowing guard recovery
common_errors.correction: Maintain knee pressure throughout the grip capture phase — only reduce pressure after the figure-four is locked and elbow is pinned

common_errors.error: Attempting to finish without controlling the opponent's elbow
common_errors.consequence: Opponent straightens their arm and extracts it from the figure-four, losing the submission entirely
common_errors.correction: Always pin the elbow to the torso or mat before applying rotational force — the elbow pin is the foundation of the kimura finish

common_errors.error: Jerking or spiking the rotation instead of applying progressive pressure
common_errors.consequence: Risk of serious shoulder injury to training partner and potential disqualification in competition
common_errors.correction: Apply rotation slowly over 3-5 seconds in training, giving the opponent clear opportunity to tap before the joint reaches its end range

common_errors.error: Lifting the opponent's arm upward instead of rotating in the shoulder plane
common_errors.consequence: Reduced mechanical advantage as the opponent can use lat and chest muscles to resist the finish
common_errors.correction: Keep the opponent's elbow pinned to their side and rotate the forearm in an arc toward their feet — lateral rotation, not vertical lifting

common_errors.error: Gripping too high on the opponent's forearm instead of at the wrist
common_errors.consequence: Shorter lever arm reduces rotational torque and makes the submission easier to defend through muscular resistance
common_errors.correction: Control at the wrist for maximum lever length — your figure-four should press against the back of their wrist joint, not mid-forearm

common_errors.error: Losing base during the grip capture transition
common_errors.consequence: Opponent sweeps or recovers guard during the moment of instability when transitioning from pressure to grip attack
common_errors.correction: Keep your base leg posted wide throughout the grip transition and maintain forward chest pressure — never sit back on your heels during the capture

training_progressions.focus: Figure-four grip capture and elbow pin
training_progressions.description: Partner offers their arm from KOB bottom position. Practice capturing the wrist, threading the figure-four, and pinning the elbow against zero resistance. Focus on hand placement, grip tightness, and smooth sequencing. Repeat 20 reps per side.

training_progressions.focus: Maintaining KOB pressure during arm capture
training_progressions.description: Establish full KOB with grips and pressure. Partner pushes against knee at 30% resistance. Practice releasing the pants grip, capturing the arm, and securing the figure-four without losing knee contact or forward pressure. Build to 50% resistance.

From secured figure-four, practice both finishing in place and stepping off to north-south. Partner provides moderate resistance and varied body positions. Develop the ability to read which finish is optimal based on opponent positioning.

training_progressions.focus: Full sequence with counters and transitions
training_progressions.description: Start from KOB with partner at 70-80% resistance. Execute the full sequence from pressure bait through grip capture to finish. When partner defends, chain to armbar, Americana, or return to KOB. Develop counter-to-counter awareness.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the Kimura from Knee on Belly primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The Kimura attacks the shoulder joint complex, specifically targeting the rotator cuff muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis), the glenohumeral ligaments, and the shoulder capsule. The forced internal rotation past the anatomical barrier creates torsional stress on these structures. Secondary stress affects the labrum and bicep tendon. The mechanism of injury is forced internal rotation beyond the shoulder's normal range of motion.

flashcards.question: Why does the Knee on Belly position provide superior leverage for the Kimura compared to side control?
flashcards.answer: The elevated hip position from KOB places the attacker's center of gravity higher than the defender's shoulder plane, allowing gravity to assist both the grip capture and the rotational finish. The top player's weight drives downward through the figure-four rather than requiring horizontal force generation. This height advantage also makes it harder for the bottom player to bridge effectively because they must lift against the concentrated knee pressure.

flashcards.question: Your opponent grabs their own belt to anchor their arm against the Kimura — what are your options?
flashcards.answer: Three primary responses exist. First, peel the grip by driving your knee across their forearm, using skeletal pressure to break their fingers' grip on the belt. Second, maintain the figure-four and step off to north-south where the angle change weakens their grip anchor. Third, redirect the attack to an Americana by reversing the rotational direction, which the belt grip does not defend against. The worst response is to fight the grip directly with arm strength.

flashcards.question: What is the breaking point indicator that tells you the Kimura is about to cause injury?
flashcards.answer: The critical indicator is when the opponent's forearm passes the plane of their back during rotation. Before this point, the shoulder has natural range of motion and the opponent can still resist. Once the forearm crosses the back plane, the rotator cuff is under maximum torsional load and injury becomes imminent. In training, apply pressure progressively and never rotate past this threshold without a tap. Additional indicators include visible grimacing and involuntary body tensing.

flashcards.question: Why is elbow control the most critical element of the Kimura finish?
flashcards.answer: The elbow must be pinned to the opponent's torso or the mat because it serves as the fulcrum of the rotational lever. Without elbow control, the opponent can straighten their arm and extract it from the figure-four, or raise their elbow to reduce the effective lever length. Pinning the elbow also prevents the opponent from rolling their shoulder forward to relieve rotational pressure. The kimura fails more often from lost elbow control than from any other single technical error.

flashcards.question: Your opponent straightens their arm as you attempt to secure the figure-four — how do you adapt?
flashcards.answer: A straightened arm is an armbar opportunity, not a failed kimura. Immediately transition by swinging your far leg over their extended arm and sitting back for an armbar finish. If the armbar angle is not available, use your body weight to re-bend their arm by driving their wrist toward their ear while threading the figure-four. The opponent's defense to one submission should open another — straightening against the kimura exposes the armbar.

flashcards.question: How should you release the Kimura after your training partner taps?
flashcards.answer: Immediately stop all rotational pressure the instant the tap is detected. Reverse the rotation slowly and return the arm toward its neutral starting position. Release the figure-four grip completely and allow your partner to self-assess their shoulder mobility before continuing. Never release suddenly or allow the arm to spring back, as this can cause injury from recoil. The release should be as controlled as the application.

flashcards.question: What grip adjustments maximize rotational torque during the Kimura finish?
flashcards.answer: Control at the wrist rather than mid-forearm to maximize the lever arm length. Position your figure-four so your forearm presses against the back of their wrist joint. Keep both elbows squeezed tight to your own body to prevent the grip from loosening. During rotation, drive your top hand toward the mat in an arc while your bottom hand pulls upward, creating a rotational couple force. Use your entire forearm as a contact surface against their wrist.

flashcards.question: When should you step off to north-south instead of finishing the Kimura in place from KOB?
flashcards.answer: Step off to north-south when the opponent has strong bridging ability, when they are actively turning into you and threatening guard recovery, or when they have created enough space that your knee is no longer effectively pinning them. North-south eliminates bridging leverage because you are perpendicular to their body. Finish in place when the opponent is flat, immobilized, and their elbow is solidly pinned — the in-place finish is faster and maintains KOB points.

flashcards.question: What is the correct plane of rotation for the Kimura finish?
flashcards.answer: The rotation should occur in the transverse plane of the shoulder — the forearm rotates laterally in an arc toward the opponent's feet while the elbow stays pinned to their side. This is internal rotation of the shoulder joint. A common error is lifting the arm upward into abduction, which allows the opponent to engage their latissimus dorsi and pectoralis muscles to resist. Keeping the rotation strictly lateral ensures maximum mechanical advantage against the weakest rotational axis.

defender.name: Kimura from Knee on Belly Defender
defender.description: Defend the Kimura from Knee on Belly in BJJ. Recognition cues, grip prevention strategies, and escape techniques to avoid the shoulder lock from bottom.
defender.overview: Defending the Kimura from Knee on Belly requires addressing two simultaneous threats: the crushing positional pressure and the shoulder lock attack. The most effective defense begins before the grip is captured, by recognizing the setup cues and keeping arms protected. Once the figure-four is locked, defensive options narrow significantly and the priority shifts to preventing the elbow pin and creating enough space to extract the arm or recover guard. The defender must understand that the attacker's primary weapon is the KOB pressure itself — it forces arm exposure. Therefore, managing the pressure through frames and hip movement is the first line of defense against the kimura, not grip fighting after the capture has occurred.
key_principles: Keep elbows tight to your body at all times under KOB pressure — arm exposure is the primary vulnerability
Address the positional pressure first through frames and hip escape before worrying about submission threats
Recognize grip capture attempts early and retract exposed arms before the figure-four is secured
If caught, prioritize preventing the elbow pin over fighting the wrist grip — a pinned elbow is the point of no return
Use bridging toward the attacker to create slack in the figure-four rather than pulling away
Maintain grip anchors on your own belt, pants, or lapel to prevent the rotational finish when caught
recognition_cues: Attacker releases their far-side pants or belt grip while maintaining KOB — this frees their hand for wrist capture
Attacker's eyes and head orient toward your far arm rather than maintaining forward pressure posture
Attacker begins shifting their weight laterally toward your far side, loading up for the grip transition
You feel increased knee pressure immediately before the grip attempt — the attacker drives harder to provoke a push reaction

defensive_options.when_to_use: Before the figure-four grip is secured — the moment you feel the attacker's hand on your wrist
defensive_options.if_successful: Attacker fails to capture the grip and must reset, returning to standard KOB with submission threat neutralized
defensive_options.risk: Focusing only on arm retraction without hip movement leaves you under full KOB pressure with no positional improvement

defensive_options.action: Bridge toward attacker and turn to knees
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the figure-four is partially secured but elbow is not yet pinned — bridge explosively toward the attacker
defensive_options.if_successful: Creates enough angle to extract the arm from the figure-four or forces the attacker off balance for guard recovery
defensive_options.risk: If the attacker maintains grip through the bridge, you may end in a worse position with the kimura still locked

defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker commits weight to the kimura attempt and reduces KOB pressure — use their offensive commitment as an escape window
defensive_options.if_successful: Recover closed guard or half guard with the attacker's grip broken, returning to a neutral guard position
defensive_options.risk: If the attacker maintains the kimura grip during guard recovery, they may finish the submission from inside your guard

defensive_options.action: Grip anchor defense by grabbing own belt or pants
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the figure-four is fully secured and elbow pin is imminent — grab your own belt or opposite lapel to create a rotational anchor
defensive_options.if_successful: Prevents the rotational finish and buys time to work other escapes while the attacker attempts to break your anchor
defensive_options.risk: This is a stalling defense that delays but does not solve the problem — the attacker will eventually break the anchor

escape_paths: Bridge toward the attacker and extract arm from the figure-four before the elbow pin is established, then immediately frame and shrimp to recover guard
Use the attacker's weight commitment to the kimura grip as an opportunity to shrimp away and recover half guard or closed guard
Roll toward the attacker in the direction of the kimura rotation to relieve shoulder pressure and scramble to turtle position

favorable_outcomes.how: When the attacker commits their weight and grips to the kimura attempt, shrimp your hips away from the knee pressure and pull them into your closed guard. The grip transition from KOB to kimura creates a window where the attacker's base is compromised.

Prevent the grip capture entirely through early recognition and arm retraction. Keep elbows tight, do not push against the knee with extended arms, and maintain defensive discipline to neutralize the submission threat.

common_errors.error: Pushing against the attacker's knee with extended arms from flat on back
common_errors.consequence: Directly exposes the far arm for figure-four capture — this is exactly the reaction the attacker is trying to provoke with KOB pressure
common_errors.correction: Keep elbows tight to body and use hip escape movement to relieve pressure rather than arm extension. Frame on the attacker's hip with your elbow, not your hand.

common_errors.error: Focusing on grip fighting after the figure-four is locked instead of addressing body position
common_errors.consequence: The attacker has mechanical advantage in the grip exchange and will eventually secure the elbow pin while you waste energy
common_errors.correction: Once caught, immediately bridge toward the attacker to create slack and work to extract the entire arm rather than fighting grip-versus-grip

common_errors.error: Pulling the captured arm away from the attacker instead of toward them
common_errors.consequence: Pulling away tightens the figure-four lock and assists the attacker's rotational force, accelerating the submission
common_errors.correction: Bridge and turn toward the attacker to create slack in the figure-four. Moving toward the submission reduces the effective rotation angle and creates extraction opportunities.

common_errors.error: Ignoring the KOB positional escape to focus solely on kimura defense
common_errors.consequence: Even if you survive the kimura attempt, you remain in a terrible position under heavy pressure with depleted energy
common_errors.correction: Integrate positional escape with submission defense — every kimura defense should simultaneously advance your guard recovery

flashcards.question: What is the earliest recognition cue that a Kimura from KOB is being set up?
flashcards.answer: The earliest cue is the attacker releasing their far-side pants or belt grip while maintaining KOB pressure. This frees their hand for the wrist capture. Additional cues include the attacker's eyes shifting toward your far arm and increased knee pressure designed to provoke a pushing reaction. Recognizing the setup before the grip is captured is the highest-percentage defense because prevention is far easier than escape.

flashcards.question: When should you tap to the Kimura from Knee on Belly?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately when you feel rotational pressure on your shoulder that you cannot reverse through technique. Do not wait for pain — once your forearm passes the plane of your back, injury is imminent. In training, tap early and often to protect your shoulder. Use verbal taps, hand taps on the attacker or mat, or foot taps. There is no shame in tapping early — shoulders do not recover quickly from rotator cuff injuries.

flashcards.question: Why is pushing the knee with extended arms the worst defensive response to KOB pressure?
flashcards.answer: Extended arms are the exact target the attacker needs for the kimura. Pushing against the knee with hands exposes the far arm for figure-four capture and creates a straight-line path for the attacker's grip. This response also wastes energy without creating escape angles because it fights pressure vertically rather than creating lateral hip movement. The correct response is to frame with elbows tight while shrimping.

flashcards.question: What direction should you bridge when caught in the Kimura from KOB?
flashcards.answer: Bridge toward the attacker, not away from them. Bridging toward the attacker creates slack in the figure-four grip and reduces the effective rotational angle on your shoulder. Bridging away tightens the lock and actually assists the attacker's finishing mechanics. This is counterintuitive but mechanically sound — moving toward the source of the rotation reduces its effectiveness and creates space to extract your arm or scramble.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying setup cues and maintaining arm protection
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes KOB and telegraphs kimura setups at slow speed. Practice recognizing the grip release cue and immediately retracting arms while initiating hip escape movement. Build pattern recognition for the attacker's weight shifts.

Partner secures the figure-four at 30% control. Practice bridging toward the attacker, creating slack, and extracting the arm. Increase resistance progressively. Focus on the counterintuitive direction of movement — toward the attacker, not away.

training_progressions.focus: Combining kimura defense with positional escape
training_progressions.description: Partner attacks kimura from KOB at 70% intensity. Practice simultaneously defending the submission while executing guard recovery sequences. Every defensive action should advance your positional escape. Chain defense into guard recovery.

training_progressions.focus: Full resistance defense from KOB bottom
training_progressions.description: Start from KOB bottom with partner attacking kimura at full competition pace. Develop automatic defensive reactions and escape timing under pressure. Focus on survival composure and technical execution under respiratory distress.
